bamo-bamo8-2019-a.title: Try small numerators
bamo-bamo8-2019-a.body:
Multiply the inequality by $11b$: we need
$$4.5\,b<11a<5b,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{11a}{5}<b<\frac{11a}{4.5}.$$
- $a=1$: $2.2<b<2.44\ldots$, no whole number $b$.
- $a=2$: $4.4<b<4.88\ldots$, no whole number $b$.
- $a=3$: $6.6<b<7.33\ldots$, so $b=7$ works, giving $a+b=10$. Check: $\frac{4.5}{11}=\frac{31.5}{77}<\frac{33}{77}=\frac37<\frac{35}{77}=\frac5{11}$. ✓
- $a\ge4$: since $\frac ab<\frac5{11}<\frac12$, we have $b>2a$, so $a+b>3a\ge12>10$.

So the smallest possible sum is $10$, reached only by $\frac37$.

**Answer: $\dfrac37$**

bamo-bamo8-2019-b.title: Split along BC
bamo-bamo8-2019-b.body:
The segment $BC$ splits $\triangle MNC$ into $\triangle BCM$ and $\triangle BCN$: since $B$ lies on $MN$, the line $BC$ separates $M$ (on $AD$, on one side of $BC$) from $N$ (on $FE$, on the other side).

- $\triangle BCM$ has base $BC$, and $M$ lies on $AD$, which is parallel to $BC$. So its height equals the height of parallelogram $ABCD$ on base $BC$, and $[BCM]=\tfrac12[ABCD]=617$.
- In the same way, $N$ lies on $FE\parallel BC$, so $[BCN]=\tfrac12[BFEC]=1402$.

So $[MNC]=617+1402=2019\text{ cm}^2$, the average of the two parallelogram areas.

**Answer: $2019\text{ cm}^2$**

bamo-bamo8-2019-b.title: Slide M and N
bamo-bamo8-2019-b.body:
Moving $M$ along $AD$ or $N$ along $FE$ does not change the areas of $\triangle BCM$ and $\triangle BCN$ (same base $BC$, same height). Slide $M$ to $D$ and $N$ to $E$: then $\triangle BCD$ is half of $ABCD$ (cut by a diagonal), and $\triangle BCE$ is half of $BFEC$. So the area is $\tfrac12(1234+2804)=2019\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: $2019\text{ cm}^2$**

bamo-bamo8-2019-c.title: Three can fail; four always work
bamo-bamo8-2019-c.body:
**Three candies are not always enough.** Three purchases use at most three kinds of coins. Imagine that the coins you happen to insert are worth $1$, $2$ and $5$ florins (whatever you choose to insert, this is possible), and that the machine always pays change in $1$-florin coins. Then you never see a $10$- or $20$-florin coin used or returned. Swapping the values of those two kinds would not change anything you observed, so you cannot tell them apart.

**Four candies are enough.** Buy four candies, paying each time with a *different* kind of coin; one kind is left unused.

1. *The 1-florin coin.* Paying with a $1$ gives no change, and every other coin gives change. If some purchase gave no change, that coin is the $1$. Otherwise the unused kind is the $1$.
2. *The 2-florin coin.* Change for a $2$ is a single $1$-florin coin. Change for $5$, $10$ or $20$ is worth at least $4$, so it is never a single $1$. So the purchase whose change was a single $1$ (if any) used the $2$; otherwise the unused kind is the $2$.
3. *The 5-florin coin.* Change for a $5$ is worth $4$ and consists only of $1$s and $2$s, which we now recognize. Change for a $10$ or $20$ is worth $9$ or $19$, so it never consists of $1$s and $2$s worth $4$ in total. So we can recognize the purchase with the $5$, if it happened; otherwise the unused kind is the $5$.
4. *The 10-florin coin.* Change for a $10$ is worth $9$ and consists of $1$s, $2$s and $5$s, all known now. Change for a $20$ that consists only of known coins is worth $19$, not $9$. So again we recognize the $10$, or it is the unused kind.
5. The remaining kind is the $20$.

**Answer: 4**

bamo-bamo8-2019-d.title: Perimeter of the gray region mod 4
bamo-bamo8-2019-d.body:
Let $L(t)$ be the perimeter (number of unit edges on the boundary) of the gray region after $t$ squares are gray. Then $L(1)=4$.

When we add a square with exactly one gray neighbor, the shared edge leaves the boundary and three new edges join it: $L$ increases by $2$. When we add a square with exactly three gray neighbors, three edges leave the boundary and one joins: $L$ decreases by $2$. So every move changes $L$ by $\pm2$, and therefore by $2\pmod 4$.

Starting from $L(1)=4\equiv0\pmod4$, we get $L(t)\equiv0$ for odd $t$ and $L(t)\equiv2\pmod4$ for even $t$. If all $64$ squares were gray, then $L(64)\equiv2\pmod 4$. But then the gray region is the whole board, whose perimeter is $32\equiv0\pmod4$. Contradiction.

**Answer: No.** ∎

bamo-bamo8-2019-e.title: The circle with diameter AC
bamo-bamo8-2019-e.body:
Let $s$ be the side of the equilateral triangle $A_1B_1C_1$.

**Step 1.** In the right triangle $AA_1C$ (right angle at $A_1$), the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse, so $B_1A_1=\tfrac12AC=B_1A=B_1C$. Hence
$$B_1A=B_1C=B_1A_1=s=B_1C_1,$$
so $A$, $C$, $A_1$, $C_1$ all lie on the circle with center $B_1$ and diameter $AC$.

**Step 2.** $C_1\ne A$: otherwise the bisector $CC_1$ would be the side $CA$, impossible. So $C_1$ is a point of this circle other than $A$ and $C$, and $\angle AC_1C=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). Thus $CC_1$ is both the angle bisector and the altitude from $C$. The triangles $ACC_1$ and $BCC_1$ then share $CC_1$ and have equal angles at $C$ and at $C_1$, so they are congruent (ASA). This gives $CA=CB$ and $AC_1=C_1B$, so $C_1$ is the midpoint of $AB$.

**Step 3.** In the right triangle $AA_1B$ (right angle at $A_1$), $A_1C_1$ is the median to the hypotenuse, so $A_1C_1=\tfrac12AB$. Therefore $AB=2s=AC$.

Together, $AB=AC=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral. ∎

bamo-bamo12-2019-4.title: Look at the largest term of a cycle
bamo-bamo12-2019-4.body:
Write $f^k$ for the $k$-th iterate. Note that if $y\ne f(y)$, then $f(f(y))\ne f(y)$: indeed $f(f(y))$ is $y+f(y)$, which differs from $f(y)$ because $y\ne0$, or $\frac{y+f(y)}{2}$, which differs from $f(y)$ because $y\ne f(y)$.

Suppose $f(x)\ne x$ for some $x$. By the remark, in the sequence $x,f(x),f^2(x),\dots$ every term differs from the next one. Since $S$ is finite, the sequence eventually repeats, so it enters a cycle $c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{L-1},c_L=c_0$ with $c_{i+1}=f(c_i)$, in which consecutive terms are distinct. Also $L\ne2$: $f(f(y))=y$ is impossible when $f(y)\ne y$, because $y+f(y)=y$ would need $f(y)=0$, and $\frac{y+f(y)}2=y$ would need $f(y)=y$. So $L\ge3$. In the cycle, each term $c_{i+2}$ is the sum or the average of $c_i$ and $c_{i+1}$.

**Normalize.** If $g(y)=-f(-y)$ on $-S$, then $g$ has the same property. So, replacing $(S,f)$ by $(-S,g)$ if necessary, we may assume that a term $M$ of the cycle with the largest absolute value is positive. Every term $c$ of the cycle then satisfies $|c|\le M$.

**The term before $M$ is positive.** Let $U,V,M$ be consecutive terms of the cycle (possible as $L\ge3$). If $V<0$, then $M=U+V$ gives $U=M-V>M$, and $M=\frac{U+V}2$ gives $U=2M-V>M$. Both contradict the maximality of $M$. So $V>0$.

**From $M$ on, everything exceeds $M/2$.** $f(M)=f(f(V))$ is $V+M$ or $\frac{V+M}{2}$, which in either case is greater than $\frac M2$. Now if two consecutive terms are greater than $\frac M2$ (and positive), then the next term, their sum or average, is also greater than $\frac M2$. Starting with $M$ and $f(M)$, every term of the cycle from $M$ onwards is greater than $\frac M2$.

**Contradiction.** Going around the cycle we come back to $M$, and $M$ is the sum or average of the two preceding terms $X$ and $Y$, both greater than $\frac M2$. A sum would be greater than $M$. An average equal to $M$, with $X,Y\le M$, forces $X=Y=M$, but consecutive terms of the cycle are distinct. Contradiction.

Hence $f(x)=x$ for all $x\in S$. ∎

bamo-bamo12-2019-5.title: Isolate n among divisors with small total
bamo-bamo12-2019-5.body:
Let $f(u)$ be the sum of the nice divisors of $u$, and $\sigma(u)$ the sum of all divisors of $u$. The idea: find a set $D$ of divisors of $n$ that contains $n$, whose other members add up to **less than $n$**, and whose nice members' sum we can compute. Then $n$ is nice if and only if the sum of the nice members of $D$ is at least $n$.

We use: $\sigma$ is multiplicative, and for a prime power, $\sigma(p^a)=\frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p-1}<p^a\cdot\frac p{p-1}$.

**$n=1$.** Ask $f(1)$: $1$ is nice iff $f(1)=1$.

**$n=p^a$ a prime power, $a\ge1$.** Ask $f(n)$. If $n$ is nice, $f(n)\ge n$. If $n$ is naughty, $f(n)\le\sigma(p^{a-1})<p^{a-1}\frac{p}{p-1}\le 2p^{a-1}\le p^a=n$. So $n$ is nice iff $f(n)\ge n$. (One question.)

**$n$ with at least two prime factors.** Write $n=p^aq^bR$, where $p<q$ are the two smallest primes dividing $n$, $a,b\ge1$, and $R$ is coprime to $pq$. Let
$$D=\{\,p^aq^br:\ r\mid R\,\},$$
the divisors of $n$ divisible by $p^aq^b$; $n\in D$.

*The members of $D$ add up to less than $2n$.* Their sum is $p^aq^b\sigma(R)$. Since $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19>10^6$, $n$ has at most $7$ distinct primes, so $R$ has at most $5$. The $i$-th smallest prime of $R$ is at least the $(i+2)$-th prime, and $\frac{x}{x-1}$ decreases in $x$, so
$$\frac{\sigma(R)}{R}<\prod_{\ell\mid R}\frac{\ell}{\ell-1}\le\frac54\cdot\frac76\cdot\frac{11}{10}\cdot\frac{13}{12}\cdot\frac{17}{16}=\frac{7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17}{9\cdot2^{10}}=\frac{17017}{9216}<2 .$$
So the members of $D$ sum to less than $2p^aq^bR=2n$, and the members other than $n$ sum to less than $n$.

*Four questions give the nice part of $D$.* A divisor of $n$ is not in $D$ exactly when its exponent of $p$ is less than $a$ (it divides $n/p$) or its exponent of $q$ is less than $b$ (it divides $n/q$). A divisor of both $n/p$ and $n/q$ is a divisor of $n/(pq)$. By inclusion–exclusion, the sum of the nice members of $D$ is
$$f(n)-f(n/p)-f(n/q)+f(n/(pq)).$$
This number is at least $n$ if $n$ is nice, and less than $n$ if $n$ is naughty.

So in every case at most four questions decide whether $n$ is nice. ∎
